questions.question: A logged-in user without the needed role calls a protected endpoint. Which status does Spring Security return?
questions.explanation: The caller is known but not allowed, which is 403. A 401 means the caller is not authenticated.

questions.question: Which check matches a user whose authority is ROLE_ADMIN?
questions.explanation: hasRole adds the ROLE_ prefix itself, so ADMIN is the correct argument.

questions.question: The role hierarchy is ROLE_ADMIN > ROLE_MANAGER > ROLE_USER, and GET /movies needs hasRole("USER"). A user with only ROLE_MANAGER calls GET /movies. What is the result?
questions.explanation: A manager includes the user role through the hierarchy, so the rule passes and the request returns 200.

questions.question: The rules are: first anyRequest().authenticated(), then requestMatchers("/reports/**").hasRole("OWNER"). A logged-in STAFF user opens /reports/sales. What happens?
options: 403, because the OWNER rule is used
200, because the first matching rule is anyRequest().authenticated()
questions.explanation: Rules are checked top to bottom and the first match wins. The broad rule comes first, so the OWNER rule is never reached.

questions.question: A team hides the Delete button from normal users in the frontend but adds no server rule for DELETE. What is the problem?
options: Nothing, because users cannot see the button
Anyone can still call the DELETE endpoint directly, so the server must enforce the role
Spring Security will block it automatically
questions.explanation: Hiding a button is not security. A direct call with curl skips the frontend, so the role must be checked on the server.
